feed.title: Quantum Computing — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Awesome Q#
entry.content:
A resource list for Q#, Microsoft’s quantum programming language. Unlike general quantum lists it focuses on one language and its toolchain.

https://github.com/ebraminio/awesome-qsharp

entry.title: Awesome Quantum Computing
entry.content:
A list of frameworks, courses and papers for quantum computing. Unlike scattered academic sources it offers both a beginner’s entry path and depth for the researcher.

https://github.com/desireevl/awesome-quantum-computing

entry.title: QPlayLearn
entry.content:
An education project explaining quantum concepts at three separate depths: game, animation and technical account. Unlike single-level resources that layering lets the same concept reach a child and an undergraduate.

https://qplaylearn.com

entry.title: Quantum Flytrap
entry.content:
A virtual lab where you assemble and run optical quantum experiments by dragging photons, polarisers and beam splitters. Unlike circuit simulators it works at the level of the physical apparatus rather than the qubit abstraction.

https://quantumflytrap.com/

entry.title: Virtual Quantum Optics Laboratory
entry.content:
A browser-based laboratory for designing and simulating quantum optics experiments. Against Quantum Flytrap it aims at research-grade accuracy rather than gamification, enough to stand in for a teaching lab.

https://www.vqol.org/

entry.title: Classiq
entry.content:
A high-level platform that synthesises quantum circuits from functional models. Unlike gate-level tools such as Qiskit, you describe what you want and the platform generates the circuit.

https://www.classiq.io

entry.title: PennyLane
entry.content:
Xanadu’s differentiable-programming framework for quantum machine learning. Unlike Qiskit it is hardware-agnostic and computes gradients automatically with PyTorch or JAX.

https://pennylane.ai

entry.title: Qiskit
entry.content:
IBM’s open-source quantum programming framework, giving access to real quantum hardware. Unlike pure simulators it runs the circuit you write on a real quantum processor over the cloud.

https://www.ibm.com/quantum/qiskit

entry.title: Quantiki
entry.content:
A long-running community wiki and resource directory on quantum computing and information. Unlike industry news sites it is academic — concept entries, conferences and job listings.

https://quantiki.org

entry.title: Quantum Algorithm Zoo
entry.content:
A comprehensive, annotated and cited catalogue of known quantum algorithms. Unlike textbooks, it lists each algorithm’s type of speed-up and original paper in one place.

https://quantumalgorithmzoo.org

entry.title: Quantum Computing Report
entry.content:
A news source tracking the quantum industry, hardware roadmaps and companies. Compared with The Quantum Insider it is more analytical; some content and databases are paid.

https://quantumcomputingreport.com

entry.title: Quantum Country
entry.content:
A site teaching quantum computing as a “book” with spaced-repetition built in. Unlike classic texts it interleaves questions so you do not forget what you read.

https://quantum.country/

entry.title: QuTiP
entry.content:
The standard open-source Python library for simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems. Unlike circuit simulators such as Qiskit, it works with continuous-time dynamics — master equations and noise — rather than gates.

https://qutip.org

entry.title: Shtetl-Optimized (Scott Aaronson)
entry.content:
The candid blog of a leading figure in quantum complexity theory. Unlike hyped quantum news it tests claims technically — for understanding what each “quantum advantage” announcement actually shows.

https://scottaaronson.blog

entry.title: The Quantum Insider
entry.content:
A news publication covering the quantum industry broadly and daily. Unlike academic sources it is industry-focused: companies, funding and product news.

https://thequantuminsider.com

entry.title: TensorFlow Quantum
entry.content:
Wraps parameterised quantum circuits as Keras-style layers to combine with classical networks. Compared with PennyLane it is tied to TensorFlow with a smaller community; one of the places hybrid classical-quantum models are explored.

https://www.tensorflow.org/quantum

entry.title: IBM Quantum
entry.content:
Queued access to real quantum processors, with circuits written and submitted through Qiskit. Unlike simulators, this is where you meet the noise and error rates they hide.

https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides

entry.title: Neden Q#?
entry.content:
Explains why quantum needs its own language. Unlike Python libraries such as Qiskit, a separate language was chosen because constraints like no-cloning and measurement collapsing state do not fit classical idioms.

https://quantum.microsoft.com/en-us/insights/blogs/qsharp/why-do-we-need-q

entry.title: LIQUi|>
entry.content:
Microsoft’s early quantum simulation platform. Unlike today’s Q# it is no longer developed; little practical value remains beyond seeing how the field’s toolchain evolved.

https://stationq.github.io/Liquid/getting-started/

entry.title: Q# Geliştirme Kiti Kurulumu
entry.content:
Installing Q# and the QDK; the VS Code extension is the shortest path to running circuits on a local simulator. Unlike IBM Quantum, you start on your own machine without any hardware access.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/install-overview-qdk

entry.title: Microsoft QDK
entry.content:
Source for the Q# compiler and simulator. Unlike the install page it shows the internals — for anyone who wants to see how a quantum circuit is compiled and simulated.

https://github.com/microsoft/qdk

entry.title: Microsoft Kuantum Yol Haritası
entry.content:
The stages from noisy intermediate-scale (NISQ) to error-corrected logical qubits. Unlike headlines it defines each stage by criteria — useful for weighing which promises are now and which a decade out, though it is a company’s roadmap.

https://quantum.microsoft.com/en-us/vision/quantum-roadmap

entry.title: Kuantum Öğrenme Kaynakları
entry.content:
A Turkish compilation of Microsoft’s quantum computing learning resources. Instead of scattered English resources, it offers an ordered way into the field.

https://azure.microsoft.com/tr-tr/resources/training-and-certifications/quantum-computing
